summary:
Kabardino-Balkaria stands under the national framework of Russia, where legal gender recognition is prohibited outright and no accessible self-determination procedure exists for trans people in the republic; ILGA-Europe's 2026 score for Russia is 2%, among the lowest in Europe.

The North Caucasus, including Kabardino-Balkaria, is treated by the UK Home Office country policy note on sexual orientation and gender identity and expression (version 2.0, June 2025) as the exception to its otherwise non-persecutory assessment of Russia: trans people and public LGBT+ advocates in the region are likely to face treatment amounting to persecution. The note documents systematic regional campaigns from 2017 to 2024 and states that the 2023 extremist designation exposes LGBT+ activity to two to six years' imprisonment, rising to six to ten years for organising, with violence spreading beyond the region.

David Isteev of North Caucasus SOS, interviewed by the Human Rights House Foundation, states that there is no safe life for LGBTIQ+ people in the North Caucasus and that even private existence can trigger violence, detention or forced return to families; he attests that conditions worsen annually.

The November 2023 Supreme Court designation of the 'international LGBT public movement' as extremist applies nationwide including Kabardino-Balkaria, making public LGBT-related expression, advocacy or display, including trans identity expression, punishable by fines, administrative detention and criminal imprisonment for participation in an extremist organisation.
tangentialFactors:
Russia's propaganda provisions were expanded in 2022 to apply regardless of age and to prohibit materials that make minors interested in gender transitions; officials have linked transition restrictions in part to draft avoidance, citing 2,700 such decisions.

Since the November 2023 ruling, individuals have been fined or jailed for displaying the rainbow flag or rainbow-coloured items, gay bar owners have been arrested with at least one dying in custody as of April 2025, and between March and May 2026 city courts outlawed nine LGBTQ organisations as extremist, including Centre T, Coming Out, Russian LGBT Network and others, with convictions of their founders for leading an extremist organisation.

Consensual same-sex sexual activity between adults has been legal since 1993 and the age of consent has been 16 since 2003 regardless of sexual orientation, but neither same-sex marriages nor civil unions are permitted, a July 2020 constitutional amendment banning same-sex marriage.
localsOnly:
Transgender residents of Kabardino-Balkaria cannot change their legal gender: the July 2023 Russian law bans both gender-affirming surgery and legal gender recognition, following April–May 2023 proposals to bar document-only gender change and to prohibit reassignment without surgery.

Russia provides no anti-discrimination protections for LGBTQ people, has no hate-crime designation based on sexual orientation, and authorities refuse to register LGBTQ organisations. A 2024 law bans adoption of Russian children by citizens or permanent residents of countries that allow gender transitions.

In Chechnya, a neighbouring North Caucasus republic, over 100 men were detained and tortured from February 2017 with at least three extrajudicial killings; a December 2018 second purge detained around 40 people with two killed, an OSCE report confirmed persecution ignored by authorities, and in March 2021 the EU sanctioned two Chechen officials accused of persecuting LGBTQ people.
outOfScopeNotes:
The source inventory contains no Kabardino-Balkaria-specific incidents of violence, arrests or prosecutions against trans people; the region-specific findings rest on the UK Home Office regional assessment and the North Caucasus SOS testimony rather than documented cases within this republic.

Whether the extremist-designation penalties cited (2–6 years, 6–10 for organising) have been applied to trans individuals specifically in Kabardino-Balkaria is not sourced.

Local facility access, healthcare provision and police practice in Kabardino-Balkaria are not covered by the inventory.
